title: Serve work in schools
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart continues his Run / Serve / Change series, which recasts leadership pressure in schools as a work-design problem rather than a shortfall of effort or expertise. This post isolates Serve work: the structural decisions a system makes once so that people are not asked to make them repeatedly under pressure. Hart distinguishes it sharply from servant leadership, arguing that relational care is often leaned on to paper over Serve work that was never done. He then walks through four domains where Serve work settles judgement at system level: a curated curriculum, a mapped assessment cycle, an evidence-grounded pedagogical framework and a timetable that expresses curriculum intent. Across all four, Serve work moves judgement upstream, reduces repeated negotiation and protects professional discretion by constraining the system rather than the individual. The piece closes with diagnostic questions leaders can ask and a short list of Serve decisions for which senior leaders are accountable.
points: Hart argues that well-done Serve work is nearly invisible: its signal is the absence of friction, with fewer emails, fewer escalations and fewer 'just to check' meetings.
Servant leadership is not Serve work; when the structural decisions are missing, leaders unwittingly ask staff to compensate with care, flexibility and personal resilience.
Serve work is framed as deciding what is fixed and what may vary, where decisions start and stop, and where the organisation absorbs complexity rather than exporting it into goodwill.
His practical diagnostic for leaders: which decisions are we still asking people to make under pressure that the system should already have settled?

Concretely, leaders are accountable for supplying curated lessons, pre-written mapped assessments and a clarified evidence-informed teaching approach instead of leaving teachers to plan, test and teach from scratch.
quotes: In schools, Run work is noisy, urgent and visible. When it fails, everyone notices.
Change work is aspirational and rhetorically familiar. It shows up in strategies, vision and improvement plans. But Serve work is different.

My take is that servant leadership is leaned on more to mitigate the effects of Serve work not having been done sufficiently. Serve work does something harder. When Serve work is missing, we unwittingly ask people to compensate with care, flexibility and resilience.
Mapped assessment points across the year are not about accountability theatre. They are about temporal coordination.

It moves judgement upstream where decisions are made deliberately, not reactively. It reduces repeated negotiation so that teachers and leaders don’t have to re-decide fundamentals under pressure. It protects professional discretion by constraining the system, not the individual.
Serve work removes unnecessary burdens by deciding once what would otherwise be negotiated repeatedly. When it is missing, schools function by consuming human capacity which leads to burnout.
